info.text: Interactive check questions for Lesson 10.2: Automated Schema Validation, CI/CD Gates, and Peer Review.

name.text: 01 Question: The Quality Assurance Gate in Textual Scholarship

questiontext.text: Why does digital scholarly editing require both automated validation and human peer review?

generalfeedback.text: A dependable digital scholarly edition requires both automated software validation and human peer review.

answer.text: Computers check rules and syntax instantly across thousands of lines, while humans provide historical judgment and paleographical insight.

feedback.text: Correct. The dual-gate approach pairs rapid machine checking of structural rules with human scholarly interpretation and contextual evaluation.

answer.text: Commercial publishing contracts legally require two software companies to sign off on files.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Quality assurance is scholarly and open-source, not dependent on commercial company signatures.

answer.text: Automated validation can only check Latin documents, requiring humans for all modern languages.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Automated XML validators check any language encoded in Unicode, but cannot judge historical truth.

answer.text: Human peer review is obsolete and only used as a backup when Internet access is unavailable.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Human peer review is essential for assessing paleography, historical context, and editorial decisions.

name.text: 02 Question: The Fragility of Local Desktop Validation

questiontext.text: What risk arises when project teams rely solely on local desktop validation on individual laptops?

generalfeedback.text: Local laptop validation is convenient for drafting, but centralized automated checks guarantee consistency across a project.

answer.text: Local software settings and schemas drift over time, hiding errors that break consistency across the project.

feedback.text: Correct. Individual laptop environments often diverge in schema paths or tool settings, leading to the "it works on my machine" trap.

answer.text: Desktop text editors automatically delete all XML files after thirty days of inactivity.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Editors like VS Code do not delete user files; the hazard is configuration divergence across team members.

answer.text: Local validation permanently damages laptop screen hardware when errors occur.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Validation is software parsing and poses no risk to computer hardware.

answer.text: Desktop computers cannot validate files containing more than fifty words.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Local editors handle large documents easily, but human inconsistency allows unvetted commits to slip through.

name.text: 03 Question: The Multi-Tiered Validation Hierarchy

questiontext.text: What are the three distinct tiers of quality control in digital textual scholarship?

generalfeedback.text: Digital editions validate across three tiers: clean syntax, structure rules, and semantic constraints.

answer.text: Tier 1 syntax (well-formedness), Tier 2 grammar (RELAX NG), and Tier 3 semantics (Schematron).

feedback.text: Correct. Validation progresses from universal XML syntax, through structural tree grammar, to context-dependent semantic business rules.

answer.text: Tier 1 word count, Tier 2 font selection, and Tier 3 print paper weight.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Those are physical typography choices, not formal XML validation tiers.

answer.text: Tier 1 spelling correction, Tier 2 language translation, and Tier 3 audio generation.

feedback.text: Incorrect. XML validation tiers evaluate formal syntactic well-formedness, schema grammar, and rule assertions.

answer.text: Tier 1 Git push, Tier 2 GitHub pull, and Tier 3 USB backup drive.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Those are version-control operations, not XML validation tiers.

name.text: 04 Question: Tier 1 Validation: XML Well-Formedness and Parser Mechanics

questiontext.text: How do XML parsers behave when encountering a syntax error, unlike web browsers rendering HTML?

generalfeedback.text: Well-formedness is the non-negotiable syntactic baseline required before any schema validation can occur.

answer.text: XML parsers enforce a strict fatal error policy and immediately stop parsing without guessing user intent.

feedback.text: Correct. Unlike lenient web browsers that attempt error recovery, XML parsers mandate strict well-formedness to ensure unambiguous tree parsing.

answer.text: XML parsers automatically correct missing tags and rewrite the user's files.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Parsers never rewrite files; they halt and report fatal syntax errors to preserve data integrity.

answer.text: XML parsers send an automated notification to local law enforcement authorities.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Parser errors are standard programming feedback, not legal infractions.

answer.text: XML parsers continue parsing and convert broken tags into emoji icons.

feedback.text: Incorrect. XML parsing halts immediately upon detecting malformed syntax.

name.text: 05 Question: Tier 2 Validation: Grammar-Based Schemas with RELAX NG

questiontext.text: What structural features does a RELAX NG schema enforce in a TEI digital edition?

generalfeedback.text: RELAX NG schemas enforce the structure rules, element ordering, and attribute types of your digital edition.

answer.text: Allowed elements, child element sequences, permitted attributes, and data types like ISO dates.

feedback.text: Correct. RELAX NG defines the formal grammar of an edition, verifying structural hierarchy and attribute constraints.

answer.text: The literary quality of the primary document's poetic metaphors.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Schemas validate formal XML structure, not the aesthetic value of historical poetry.

answer.text: The market resale value of the physical manuscript at auction.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Schemas evaluate digital data formatting, not commercial manuscript valuations.

answer.text: The physical weight of the paper used in the author's laptop printer.

feedback.text: Incorrect. RELAX NG is a digital schema language with no connection to printer paper specifications.

name.text: 06 Question: The Limits of Grammar: What RELAX NG Cannot Catch

questiontext.text: Which type of editorial constraint exceeds the capabilities of pure RELAX NG grammar schemas?

generalfeedback.text: Grammar schemas cannot enforce cross-element conditional rules, creating the need for rule-based Schematron validation.

answer.text: Conditional rules across elements, such as requiring `@ref` when `type="deputy"` or matching `@orig` with `@reg`.

feedback.text: Correct. Grammar schemas evaluate elements in isolation and cannot easily enforce conditional co-occurrence rules or cross-references.

answer.text: Checking whether an element has a closing tag.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Checking closing tags is basic Tier 1 well-formedness handled by all XML parsers.

answer.text: Checking whether element names use uppercase or lowercase letters.

feedback.text: Incorrect. RELAX NG schemas easily enforce exact case sensitivity on element names.

answer.text: Detecting whether a file is saved on a hard drive or a USB thumb drive.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Schemas validate text contents, not storage drive hardware types.

name.text: 07 Question: Tier 3 Validation: ISO Schematron (ISO/IEC 19757-3)

questiontext.text: How does Schematron differ from RELAX NG in evaluating XML documents?

generalfeedback.text: Schematron uses XPath to enforce project-specific editorial rules and emit plain-language error messages.

answer.text: Schematron uses XPath to query targeted patterns and test assertions, outputting human-authored error messages.

feedback.text: Correct. Schematron selects nodes using XPath expressions and tests specific conditions, reporting friendly project-specific errors.

answer.text: Schematron converts all XML files into relational SQL database tables.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Schematron is an XML validation language, not a database transformation utility.

answer.text: Schematron requires an active subscription to commercial cloud software.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Schematron is an open ISO standard that runs locally with open-source tools.

answer.text: Schematron only runs on documents written in Classical Greek.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Schematron validates any well-formed XML document regardless of language.

name.text: 08 Question: Authoring Schematron Rules for Scholarly Editions

questiontext.text: What is the function of the `` element in a Schematron rule?

generalfeedback.text: Schematron patterns select target elements and test assertions, guiding editors with helpful error messages.

answer.text: It defines a mandatory test condition that must be true; if false, its human-readable error message is displayed.

feedback.text: Correct. The `assert` element tests an XPath condition and prints its enclosed message whenever that condition evaluates to false.

answer.text: It automatically generates digital images of missing manuscript folios.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Schematron tests text rules; it does not generate visual imagery.

answer.text: It deletes any XML tag that contains spelling mistakes.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Schematron reports validation warnings but does not delete user markup.

answer.text: It encrypts the document so that peer reviewers cannot read it.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Schematron is a transparent testing tool that facilitates open peer review.

name.text: 09 Question: Enforcing Cross-Reference and Identifier Integrity

questiontext.text: How does Schematron protect identifier integrity across a digital edition?

generalfeedback.text: Schematron rules verify that all internal links and person references resolve to defined identifiers in your edition.

answer.text: It verifies that internal pointers like `@ref="#cope"` resolve to matching `xml:id` definitions in the ``.

feedback.text: Correct. Schematron uses XPath to ensure every internal hash reference points to an existing defined identifier in the document.

answer.text: It prevents students from using personal pronouns in their essays.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Schematron verifies XML attribute pointers, not essay writing style.

answer.text: It assigns random serial numbers to every paragraph on the page.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Schematron tests existing attributes; it does not inject random serial numbers.

answer.text: It removes all hyperlinks to external library websites.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Schematron verifies link validity rather than removing links.

name.text: 10 Question: Validating Linguistic and Attribute Co-Occurrences

questiontext.text: Why is Schematron valuable for auditing grammatical lemmatization markup in `` tags?

generalfeedback.text: Schematron guards linguistic annotations by checking that words carry canonical lemmas and valid part-of-speech codes.

answer.text: It confirms that words marked as verbs or nouns carry non-empty canonical lemmas and valid part-of-speech codes.

feedback.text: Correct. Schematron verifies that linguistic attributes like `@lemma` and `@pos` are consistently populated and conform to approved whitelists.

answer.text: It translates historical verbs into colloquial modern slang.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Schematron validates grammatical annotation consistency; it does not modernize historical vocabulary.

answer.text: It counts the number of letters in every word and reorders them alphabetically.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Schematron checks markup rules without altering text order.

answer.text: It forbids editors from tagging more than ten verbs per manuscript page.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Schematron enforces data quality rather than arbitrary quantitative caps.

name.text: 11 Question: Compiling and Executing Schematron via XSLT Engines

questiontext.text: Which command-line utility is standard for executing RELAX NG and Schematron validation in terminal workflows?

generalfeedback.text: Tools like Jing execute Schematron rules on the command line, enabling automated validation in scripts and CI pipelines.

answer.text: `jing`

feedback.text: Correct. James Clark's open-source `jing` validator processes both RELAX NG schemas and Schematron rule files directly in the terminal.

answer.text: `photoshop`

feedback.text: Incorrect. Adobe Photoshop is an image manipulation program, not an XML schema validator.

answer.text: `curl`

feedback.text: Incorrect. `curl` transfers data across network protocols; it does not validate XML schemas.

answer.text: `ping`

feedback.text: Incorrect. `ping` tests network connectivity between computers, not XML validation.

name.text: 12 Question: Introduction to Continuous Integration (CI/CD) for Digital Humanities

questiontext.text: What is the primary function of Continuous Integration in a collaborative digital edition?

generalfeedback.text: Continuous Integration automatically tests every commit in the cloud, guaranteeing that broken files never go unnoticed.

answer.text: Automatically running tests and validation checks on a cloud server whenever commits are pushed to the repository.

feedback.text: Correct. CI acts as an automated gatekeeper, testing every commit to ensure broken markup or invalid schemas are detected immediately.

answer.text: Automatically printing physical paper books and shipping them to local bookstores.

feedback.text: Incorrect. CI automates software testing and digital builds, not physical commercial distribution.

answer.text: Replacing human historians with automated conversational chatbots.

feedback.text: Incorrect. CI provides technical quality control to support human scholars, not replace them.

answer.text: Preventing team members from making commits outside of scheduled class hours.

feedback.text: Incorrect. CI runs anytime a commit is pushed, supporting asynchronous collaboration.

name.text: 13 Question: Anatomy of a GitHub Actions Workflow

questiontext.text: Where are GitHub Actions workflows configured inside a project repository?

generalfeedback.text: GitHub Actions workflows are version-controlled YAML files that define automated testing triggers and commands.

answer.text: Inside `.github/workflows/` as human-readable YAML configuration files.

feedback.text: Correct. Workflows live in `.github/workflows/*.yml`, version-controlled right alongside your edition source text.

answer.text: Inside the computer's BIOS firmware chip.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Workflows are standard text files stored in the Git repository.

answer.text: Inside an unversioned Word document saved on the instructor's desktop.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Workflows must be saved inside `.github/workflows/` so GitHub can execute them automatically.

answer.text: Inside a temporary browser cookie that expires after twenty minutes.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Workflows are permanent repository assets tracked in Git history.

name.text: 14 Question: Writing a Complete TEI Validation Workflow

questiontext.text: What sequence of actions does a basic TEI validation workflow execute on GitHub Actions?

generalfeedback.text: A twenty-line YAML file configures GitHub Actions. It installs XML tools and tests your files on every push.

answer.text: Checking out the repository code, installing XML tools like `libxml2-utils` and `jing`, and running `xmllint` and schema checks.

feedback.text: Correct. A standard workflow checks out files, sets up command-line validators, and tests the XML for well-formedness and schema validity.

answer.text: Formatting the hard drive, reinstalling the operating system, and shutting down the server.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Workflows run harmless software checks inside isolated cloud containers.

answer.text: Downloading video games and broadcasting live streams to social media.

feedback.text: Incorrect. GitHub Actions runners execute specified testing commands for project validation.

answer.text: Translating the repository into Morse code and transmitting it over radio waves.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The workflow tests XML files using standard command-line tools.

name.text: 15 Question: Integrating Community Validation Actions

questiontext.text: Why is fetching canonical schemas directly from authoritative URLs advantageous in CI workflows?

generalfeedback.text: Community actions and remote schema downloads keep repository sizes small while validating against official TEI releases.

answer.text: It keeps repository file sizes small while guaranteeing validation against official international TEI P5 releases.

feedback.text: Correct. Downloading official schemas during workflow runs prevents bloat in your repository and ensures tests use canonical definitions.

answer.text: It prevents classmates from viewing your repository source code.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Remote schema fetching does not alter repository visibility settings.

answer.text: It eliminates the need to write TEI XML tags in your document.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Schemas validate XML tags; they do not write markup for you.

answer.text: It charges commercial licensing fees to the university department.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Official TEI schemas are completely free and open-source.

name.text: 16 Question: Associating Documents and Schemas: `<?xml-model?>`

questiontext.text: Where should `` processing instructions be placed within a TEI document?

generalfeedback.text: The xml-model processing instruction links both Relax NG and Schematron schemas directly inside the XML document header.

answer.text: At the very top of the file, immediately after the XML declaration and before the root `` element.

feedback.text: Correct. Processing instructions belong in the file prolog before the root element so editors and tools can discover schemas.

answer.text: Inside the `` revision log as a `` entry.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Processing instructions belong in the file prolog before ``, not inside child elements.

answer.text: At the very end of the file, after the closing `` tag.

feedback.text: Incorrect. XML parsers require all content except comments to precede or exist inside the single root element.

answer.text: Inside an external CSS stylesheet file.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The `` declaration is an XML processing instruction that lives in the XML document itself.

name.text: 17 Question: Converting CI Failures to Inline GitHub Annotations

questiontext.text: How does GitHub Actions display validation failures to pull request reviewers?

generalfeedback.text: GitHub CI automatically displays validation errors as inline visual annotations on the exact lines that caused the failure.

answer.text: As visual inline annotations highlighting the exact line of code where the error occurred in the diff.

feedback.text: Correct. GitHub translates compiler errors into clickable inline badges directly on conflicted or failing lines.

answer.text: By sending a physical printed postcard through the postal service.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Alerts are displayed digitally within the web pull request interface.

answer.text: By locking the user out of their computer operating system.

feedback.text: Incorrect. CI errors are informational warnings displayed within GitHub.

answer.text: By deleting the pull request automatically without saving logs.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Pull requests remain open and preserve detailed logs so authors can inspect and fix errors.

name.text: 18 Question: Protecting Branches with Automated CI Merge Gates

questiontext.text: How do Branch Protection Rules prevent broken XML from reaching production editions?

generalfeedback.text: Branch protection rules disable the merge button until all automated validation tests pass with zero errors.

answer.text: They disable the green "Merge" button on pull requests until all required automated validation checks pass with zero errors.

feedback.text: Correct. Protection rules enforce quality gates, ensuring that failing or invalid code cannot be merged into the master branch.

answer.text: They delete the entire repository whenever a student types a syntax error.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Branch protection guards the main branch; it never deletes repositories.

answer.text: They require students to pay a cash deposit before creating a branch.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Branch protection is a free repository security setting.

answer.text: They prevent instructors from viewing student homework submissions.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Branch protection enforces merge criteria; it does not restrict read access.

name.text: 19 Question: Automated Preview and Artifact Compilation in CI

questiontext.text: In addition to validation, what artifact compilation tasks can GitHub Actions automate upon merge?

generalfeedback.text: CI workflows can automatically transform raw TEI XML into web reading views and publish them live to GitHub Pages.

answer.text: Transforming TEI XML into HTML reading views and deploying preview websites live to GitHub Pages.

feedback.text: Correct. CI pipelines can run stylesheet transformations and publish static web previews automatically whenever main updates.

answer.text: Mining cryptocurrency tokens in the background on university servers.

feedback.text: Incorrect. University and GitHub policies strictly forbid cryptocurrency mining.

answer.text: Purchasing physical antique parchment from rare manuscript dealers.

feedback.text: Incorrect. CI workflows execute computational file processing, not commercial purchases.

answer.text: Deleting all previous versions of the primary manuscript image.

feedback.text: Incorrect. CI workflows build derivative reading views while preserving all source assets.

name.text: 20 Question: The Boundary Between Automated Linting and Human Peer Review

questiontext.text: What critical dimension of digital scholarship can human peer reviewers assess that automated linters cannot?

generalfeedback.text: Software enforces mechanical validity, freeing human scholars to focus on paleographical judgment and historical interpretation.

answer.text: Whether the transcription accurately represents the physical manuscript handwriting and historical context.

feedback.text: Correct. Linters check syntactic and schema rules; only human scholars can judge paleographical readings and historical accuracy.

answer.text: Whether the file contains balanced angle brackets.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Automated linters easily verify balanced angle brackets and XML well-formedness.

answer.text: Whether the file was saved with UTF-8 character encoding.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Character encoding is easily checked and verified by automated tools.

answer.text: Whether the file has an `.xml` extension.

feedback.text: Incorrect. File extensions are trivial for software to inspect.

name.text: 21 Question: Designing a Structured TEI Peer-Review Rubric

questiontext.text: What four editorial layers should a structured peer-review rubric evaluate in our seminar editions?

generalfeedback.text: A structured four-layer rubric ensures that peer review evaluates metadata, diplomatic fidelity, normalization, and entity markup.

answer.text: Metadata and codicology, diplomatic transcription fidelity, editorial normalization, and named-entity markup.

feedback.text: Correct. A complete scholarly audit examines the teiHeader, facsimile alignment, regularized choice tags, and entity links.

answer.text: Screen resolution, internet download speed, keyboard model, and mouse sensitivity.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Those are hardware specifications, not scholarly digital edition criteria.

answer.text: Page count, font color, printer paper size, and bookbinding glue.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Those are physical manufacturing features, not digital philology layers.

answer.text: Spelling, grammar, punctuation, and word count of personal diary entries.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The rubric evaluates structured TEI encoding layers and manuscript evidence.

name.text: 22 Question: Auditing the `teiHeader` and Provenance Layer

questiontext.text: What essential information must be confirmed when auditing an edition's ``?

generalfeedback.text: Auditing the teiHeader verifies that physical holding archives, licenses, and revision histories are thoroughly documented.

answer.text: The holding archive, physical shelfmark, material support, and historical date of the primary witness.

feedback.text: Correct. The `sourceDesc` must thoroughly document the physical artifact and holding institution to ensure scholarly citable provenance.

answer.text: The retail purchase price of the laptop used by the student transcriber.

feedback.text: Incorrect. `sourceDesc` describes the historical manuscript artifact, not modern laptop equipment.

answer.text: The personal home address of the archive security guard.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Personal staff addresses should never be included; privacy must be protected.

answer.text: The weather forecast in Paris or Halifax on the day the file was committed.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Meteorological forecasts are irrelevant to archival witness identification.

name.text: 23 Question: Auditing Diplomatic Transcription and Physical Milestones

questiontext.text: What is a primary task when auditing diplomatic transcription against high-resolution facsimiles?

generalfeedback.text: Auditing diplomatic transcription requires comparing every character, line break, and unclear stroke against high-resolution facsimiles.

answer.text: Verifying that every line break `` matches a physical line on the page and that damaged strokes are tagged with ``.

feedback.text: Correct. Reviewers compare transcribed text line by line against visual facsimiles, checking lineation and damage markup.

answer.text: Replacing all historical handwriting with modern computerized cursive fonts.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Diplomatic auditing verifies transcription accuracy, not font replacement.

answer.text: Deleting all line breaks to convert the historical document into a single long sentence.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Diplomatic editions strictly preserve physical line breaks using `` milestones.

answer.text: Cropping the manuscript image to remove all historical marginalia.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Marginalia provide crucial codicological evidence and must be preserved.

name.text: 24 Question: Auditing Normalization, Rendering, and Stylesheets

questiontext.text: What should a reviewer check when evaluating editorial regularizations in `` tags?

generalfeedback.text: Auditing normalization ensures that historical spelling choices are linguistically sound and render clearly in stylesheets.

answer.text: That `` and `` pairs are symmetric, historically defensible, and render clearly in reading stylesheets.

feedback.text: Correct. Reviewers verify that historical forms and regularized readings are balanced, justified by policy, and displayed well in CSS.

answer.text: That all historical spellings have been erased from the XML file permanently.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI `` preserves both original historical spelling and regularized form side by side.

answer.text: That the stylesheet only displays text in bright neon pink.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Reading stylesheets should prioritize legibility and scholarly clarity.

answer.text: That regularized words are translated into ancient Egyptian hieroglyphs.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Regularization normalizes historical orthography within the same language.

name.text: 25 Question: Auditing Linguistic Markup and Named Entities

questiontext.text: Why must reviewers test authority links (`@ref`) attached to `` and `` tags?

generalfeedback.text: Auditing linguistic and entity markup confirms that lemmas are canonical and authority links resolve to verified records.

answer.text: To ensure that links resolve to verified real-world entities in databases like VIAF, GeoNames, or Wikidata.

feedback.text: Correct. A broken or mismatched authority link corrupts the edition's connection to the Linked Open Data cloud.

answer.text: To verify that the historical figures are currently active on social media platforms.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Authority records identify historical persons; they do not check contemporary social media accounts.

answer.text: To ensure that external websites pay advertising commissions to the university.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Linked Open Data authorities are non-profit public academic infrastructure.

answer.text: To confirm that all personal names are written entirely in capital letters.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Capitalization preserves historical or canonical orthography; authority links verify entity identity.

name.text: 26 Question: Executing the In-Class Peer Review Exchange

questiontext.text: What is the final step in the four-step peer review exchange protocol?

generalfeedback.text: The in-class peer review exchange allows students to test each other's editions against automated checks and scholarly rubrics.

answer.text: Opening constructive GitHub Issues or inline PR comments with specific praise and actionable suggestions.

feedback.text: Correct. Reviewers synthesize their audit into clear, actionable feedback on GitHub to help their classmates improve their editions.

answer.text: Deleting the partner's repository from GitHub to prevent competition.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Peer review is collaborative and supportive; deleting classmate work is strictly forbidden.

answer.text: Refusing to speak to classmates until the end of the academic year.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The peer review exchange fosters active discussion and shared problem-solving.

answer.text: Writing a negative review on public social media rating websites.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Scholarly reviews are conducted professionally within project repositories.

name.text: 27 Question: Case Study: Digital Scholarly Publishing and Traveling Validation

questiontext.text: What is the "Traveling Imprimatur" developed by the Digital Latin Library?

generalfeedback.text: Major publishing platforms like the Digital Latin Library use automated CI pipelines as formal gateways to scholarly publication.

answer.text: An automated CI pipeline that tests XML files against strict schemas, certifying passing editions with a digital imprimatur.

feedback.text: Correct. The DLL uses automated CI validation as a prerequisite for formal peer review and scholarly publication.

answer.text: A physical rubber stamp mailed to authors by post.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The Traveling Imprimatur is an automated digital certification pipeline.

answer.text: A commercial copyright license sold to students for profit.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The DLL is an open-access non-profit scholarly publishing platform.

answer.text: A software program that automatically translates Latin into French.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The DLL publishes critical Latin editions; the imprimatur certifies XML validity.

name.text: 28 Question: Digital Longevity and the Endings Project Principles

questiontext.text: Why does The Endings Project recommend building digital editions using static files rather than server databases?

generalfeedback.text: The Endings Project principles mandate static, open-standard files to ensure digital editions survive for decades without maintenance.

answer.text: Static HTML, CSS, and TEI XML files survive for decades without database maintenance, security patches, or server upgrades.

feedback.text: Correct. Static files eliminate database obsolescence and security vulnerabilities, ensuring twenty-year digital longevity.

answer.text: Static files automatically generate money for university endowments.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The Endings Project focuses on long-term preservation and digital survival, not monetization.

answer.text: Server databases are illegal under Canadian intellectual property legislation.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Databases are legal; the issue is that complex dynamic servers require continuous maintenance and decay quickly.

answer.text: Static files can only be read on computers manufactured before 1995.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Static web standards are supported by all modern and future web browsers.

name.text: 29 Question: Archiving, Persistent Identification, and FAIR Data

questiontext.text: What scholarly benefit does depositing a repository release in Zenodo provide?

generalfeedback.text: Archiving releases to Zenodo mints permanent DOIs. It guarantees long-term preservation.

answer.text: It mints a permanent Digital Object Identifier (DOI) and guarantees long-term bit-level preservation in academic archives.

feedback.text: Correct. Zenodo provides persistent DOIs and archival storage, ensuring your edition is permanently findable and citable.

answer.text: It automatically registers the student for graduate school admission.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Zenodo is an open research archive, not a university admissions office.

answer.text: It deletes the repository from GitHub to save cloud storage space.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Zenodo archives a snapshot while your GitHub repository remains active for ongoing work.

answer.text: It prevents anyone from reading your edition without paying a fee.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Zenodo supports open-access research data sharing under FAIR principles.

name.text: 30 Question: The Consolidated Milestone: Looking Ahead to Final Publication

questiontext.text: What milestone does completing Module 10 represent in the RELS 398 curriculum?

generalfeedback.text: Completing the consolidation milestone unites nine editorial layers under automated CI gates, preparing your edition for publication.

answer.text: All nine accumulated layers are validated under automated CI gates, preparing the edition for publication and interface design.

feedback.text: Correct. Consolidation completes the foundational encoding phase, setting the stage for advanced publication and public presentation.

answer.text: Students graduate immediately and no further coursework is required.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Phase 3 (Advanced Publication and Presentation) begins next week in Module 11.

answer.text: The primary manuscript witnesses are returned to museum archives and never used again.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The digitized editions continue into Phase 3 for web styling and interactive publication.

answer.text: All TEI XML files are deleted to make room for final exam review notes.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The consolidated XML files are the primary assets that will be published in Modules 11 through 13.
